title: Dhul Hijjah at home
hook: many who plan to sacrifice don't cut hair or nails in the first ten (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhul Qa'dah, the month of packing and goodbyes. Your line was the pilgrims set out. Did you settle one small thing, the way a traveler would? Now they've arrived. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-four.

The new moon of Dhul Hijjah is sighted. Far away, the pilgrims are in Makkah in their white cloth. And in a bathroom in an ordinary house, a pair of nail clippers goes into a drawer and stays there. A haircut gets moved to later in the month. Nobody here is on hajj. They haven't left town. So why is someone at home suddenly not cutting their nails? It goes back to one hadith in Sahih Muslim, and to a question anyone who stays behind might ask: how do I take part in a journey I'm not on?
screen: `THE NEW MOON OF DHUL HIJJAH.` → `CLIPPERS IN A DRAWER.` → `TAKING PART FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Start with the hadith. Umm Salamah, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, reports his words in Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase: when the ten days begin, and one of you intends to offer a sacrifice, let him leave his hair and his skin alone. Not a big act. A small holding back, for someone planning the sacrifice of the coming Eid. Schools of law differ on how binding it is: some treat it as required, some as recommended, and some don't require it. Second, why it matters. The pilgrims in ihram have their own list of things they leave alone, and cutting hair and nails is on it. Some scholars point out the echo. At home, a person keeps one small piece of what the pilgrim is keeping. Home, but with them. Third, the days themselves. In al-Bukhari, Ibn 'Abbas reports the Prophet saying, in paraphrase, that no good deeds are dearer to Allah than those done in these ten days. They asked: not even striving in Allah's path? He said: not even that, except a person who goes out with himself and his wealth and comes back with nothing. These are days for everyone, not only the travelers. Fourth, a sound you might hear. Al-Bukhari mentions that Ibn 'Umar and Abu Hurayrah would go out to the market in these ten days saying Allahu akbar, and people would say it along with them. And on the day of 'Arafah, when the pilgrims stand on the plain, some people at home fast. Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet's hope that this fast wipes away the sins of the year before it and the year after it.
screen: `LEAVE HAIR AND NAILS ALONE.` · `AN ECHO OF THE PILGRIM'S IHRAM.` · `NO DEEDS DEARER THAN IN THESE DAYS.` · `TAKBIR IN THE MARKET, A FAST AT HOME.`

segments.voice: The practice: keep one small restraint. Settle, and breathe. Choose one tiny thing to leave alone for a while. Not something dramatic. Hitting snooze. A purchase you don't need. A comment you'd usually make. Let it be small enough to keep. Now, each time you notice yourself not doing it, let that moment point somewhere: to someone far away who is keeping much more. If you pray, you can remember the pilgrims each time. If you don't, simply notice the space the small restraint opens up. The bell holds the time.
Dhul Hijjah at home. The month of the pilgrimage, kept by those who stay behind: a small restraint, good deeds in the ten days, takbir, and the fast of 'Arafah. Today's word.

Your line: home, but with them. Today, keep your one small restraint, and let every time you keep it be a thought sent toward someone far away. Tomorrow, Eid al-Adha. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: In the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah, Muslims at home often increase prayer, charity and takbir, and some fast on the day of 'Arafah; those who intend to offer a sacrifice for Eid al-Adha often leave their hair and nails uncut until it is done, following a hadith in Sahih Muslim.

notes: Schools differ on the hair-and-nails restraint (e.g., Hanbalis generally hold it obligatory, Shafi'is recommended, Hanafis not required); the script says only 'some treat it as required, others as recommended'. Confirm the framing is fair.
'Some scholars point out the echo' between this restraint and the pilgrim's ihram: confirm.
The Ibn 'Umar and Abu Hurayrah report is a chapter note (mu'allaq) in al-Bukhari; confirm the reference and that it refers to the ten days.
'People at home often fast' on 'Arafah: softened from any count; confirm.
